hero.title: Venerdì
hero.lead: You land in the morning. The other two land at night. This is the plan for everything in between.

rules.title: Legs first
rules.body: Sunday is 21.1 km, so Friday's walking stays under 10 km. The one real hill gets a taxi.

rules.title: Carbs are training
rules.body: Supplì, pizza bianca, carbonara. All of it counts as carb-loading if you squint.

rules.title: Coffee at the counter
rules.body: Romans drink it standing at the bar. Sit at a table and the same coffee can cost three times as much.

rules.title: Zero alcohol
rules.body: Nobody will miss it. Every bar has Crodino and Sanbittèr, the bitter orange aperitivo minus the booze.

arrival.title: Getting in
arrival.lead: Wherever you land, drop your bag off first, then we ease in. From Termini, bus 40 or 64 to the Argentina stop takes about 20 minutes.

options.detail: 32 min non-stop, every 15 min, first train 05:38. €14. Tap your card or phone on the platform reader, no ticket needed.
€8. Doesn't go to Termini; stops at Trastevere and Ostiense instead.

options.how: Terravision or SIT coach to Termini

options.detail: €55 from Fiumicino, €40 from Ciampino, to anywhere inside the old walls. Say 'tariffa fissa'. Ignore anyone offering a ride inside the terminal.

arrival.warning: Flying easyJet? Italy's strike register lists a 24-hour easyJet cabin-crew strike on 16 October. Check the app on Thursday.

stops.title: Maritozzo, standing up
stops.body: Rome's breakfast is a soft bun split open and stuffed with so much whipped cream it won't close. Order at the counter and eat it standing up. Cream on your nose is part of it.
stops.move: Say 'un maritozzo e un cappuccino al banco'. They fill it with cream when you order (custard and chocolate also exist).

swaps.title: Coming in through Termini?
swaps.body: The maritozzo half of Rome swears by, 8 minutes' walk from the station. Open from 06:30, closed Tuesdays.

stops.title: Caesar was stabbed here. Now it's cats.
stops.body: A sunken square of 2,000-year-old temples in the middle of traffic. Julius Caesar was killed in the Curia of Pompey, on the west side. These days a colony of cats sleeps on the columns.
stops.move: Walk the railing all the way round. The cat shelter on the Via Florida corner only opens at noon, so this morning it's railing views.

stops.title: The dome that isn't there
stops.body: The church never got its dome. So in 1685 Andrea Pozzo painted one on a flat canvas, and from the right spot your brain completely buys it. Then walk towards the altar and watch it fall apart. There's a big mirror on the floor so you can study the ceiling without wrecking your neck.
stops.move: Find the small marble disc in the middle of the nave and stand on it.

stops.title: Coffee, round two
stops.body: The gran caffè comes already sweetened, with a thick foam on top, and they guard the recipe. Pay at the till first, then hand the receipt to the barista.
stops.move: Say 'amaro' if you want it without sugar.

stops.title: Look up
stops.body: A concrete dome from around 125 AD with a nine-metre hole in the top, and it's still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Walk in and stand right under the hole. If it rains, even better: the rain falls right through and drains out of little holes in the floor.
stops.move: Raphael is buried on the left side. The tickets are named and checked against ID: I'm booking the 11:00–12:00 slot for both of us, so bring a passport or ID card.

plaque.street: Piazza di S. Luigi de' Francesi

stops.title: A free Caravaggio
stops.body: Back left chapel: three huge paintings of St Matthew. In the famous one, a beam of light cuts across a table of guys counting money, and Jesus points at one of them. A bearded man points back like 'who, me?'. Or he's pointing at the kid next to him. Art historians still argue about it.
stops.move: The church shuts for lunch at 12:45, so this one doesn't wait. No coins needed any more: the chapel got new lighting in 2025.

stops.title: A stadium, still
stops.body: It's long and rounded at one end because it's built exactly on top of a Roman stadium. Walk it end to end, past Bernini's four river gods, then grab a ride south.
stops.move: Don't eat on the square itself. Five minutes away, everything is better and cheaper.

transferToNext.note: Bus 30 (every 10 min) from the Rinascimento stop, direction Laurentina: 12 min to Marmorata/Vanvitelli, then 8 min on foot. Taxi about €12–15.

stops.title: Lunch at the market
stops.body: A covered neighbourhood market with fruit stalls, butchers and a handful of counters doing lunch. Mordi e Vai makes the one sandwich to get: panino all'allesso, slow-cooked beef in a roll dipped in its own broth. Then split a trapizzino, a triangle of pizza bread stuffed with something stewed, from the shop around the corner where it was invented.
stops.move: At Mordi e Vai, take a number. Bring cash, don't wear white, and be eating by 13:15: the good stalls sell out.

swaps.title: Staying central instead?
swaps.body: Fried rice balls with a mozzarella core at Supplizio, then pizza bianca by the slice at Roscioli's bakery. Both cheap, both 5 minutes from Navona.

swaps.title: Gelato nearby
swaps.body: A neighbourhood gelateria since 1986, five minutes from the market. If it's open, it's a bonus.

stops.title: A pyramid, two poets, lots of cats
stops.body: Rome has a pyramid. A rich magistrate built it as his tomb around 12 BC, and behind it is the calmest garden in the city. Keats is buried here under a stone that doesn't even carry his name: 'Here lies One Whose Name was writ in Water'. Shelley is up by the old wall, next to a stone angel collapsed in grief. And there are cats, because there's a whole colony living by the pyramid.
stops.move: Go left into the Old Cemetery for Keats with the pyramid right behind him. They ask for €5 each at the gate, and a couple of photos is fine, just not for social media.

rain.title: Statues in a power plant
rain.body: Rome's weirdest museum: marble gods and emperors standing in front of giant diesel engines and turbines in the city's first power station. Nearly empty, and an hour covers it. One Metro B stop from Piramide to Garbatella, then a short walk.
rain.move: Head straight for the engine hall.

transferIn.note: Walk 10 minutes to Piramide, one stop to Garbatella, then 7 minutes on foot.

stops.title: Pick up the bibs
stops.body: The race village is right next to Eataly Ostiense. Grabbing the bibs today means Saturday is free for doing nothing. Anyone can walk in, there are running brands and free stuff, Gemelli hospital does free health checks, and Eataly has snacks.
stops.move: Each of us needs the confirmation letter (download it from the race site, print it, check for the two green OKs and our wave time) and photo ID. From Piramide, take the underpass towards Ostiense station and Eataly instead of crossing the big square.

transferToNext.note: The Aventine is the day's only real hill. A taxi up is about €10. Walking it is 1.9 km and 25 minutes: flat until the last stretch, then 30 m up Via di Porta Lavernale.

stops.title: Look through the keyhole
stops.body: There's a green door with a queue in front of it. Put your eye to the keyhole and you get a perfect hedge tunnel ending in St Peter's dome. You're standing in Italy, looking through the Knights of Malta's garden, at a dome in the Vatican.
stops.move: Phone at 1x, lens right on the hole, tap the dome to fix the exposure. More than about 20 people in line? Do Santa Sabina first and come back, and skip it if it's still long at 16:25. Santa Sabina is 3 minutes away: a small window in its porch shows an orange tree said to come from a seed St Dominic brought from Spain around 1220. Most people walk right past it.

stops.title: The light goes gold
stops.body: A walled garden of orange trees with a terrace at the end, and all of Rome below it. Around five the light starts turning, and the domes go from white to honey. On a Friday afternoon it's mostly locals and their dogs.
stops.move: Walk the avenue to the belvedere at the far end. The gates close at 18:00, before sunset, so around 17:10 we take Clivo di Rocca Savella down: an old cobbled lane, downhill all the way. If that gate is shut, use the main gate and Clivo dei Publicii (10 min).

rain.title: A corridor that lies
rain.body: Borromini's colonnade looks like a long gallery with a full-size statue at the end. It's less than 9 metres deep and the statue is small. It's two minutes from Campo de' Fiori, and Antico Forno Roscioli around the corner does pizza bianca for the road.
rain.move: You see the colonnade from the courtyard; last access to it is 18:30. Skip the picture rooms upstairs.

transferIn.note: From the keyhole, about €10. Skip the Orange Garden in the rain.

stops.title: The medieval lie detector
stops.body: A giant marble face in a church porch. Legend says it bites the hand of anyone who lies. If the queue is short, do it. If it isn't, look through the gate, then at the two Roman temples across the road.
stops.move: Only worth it with fewer than ten people in line. It shuts at 17:50.

stops.title: Sunset from the typewriter
stops.body: Romans call the giant white monument on Piazza Venezia 'the typewriter', and mostly complain about it. But a glass lift goes to the very top, and from up there you see the whole city, 360 degrees. Sunset is at 18:29, and the sun drops right behind the Gianicolo. Stay for blue hour, when the lights come on over the Forum.
stops.move: Walk in at the main Piazza Venezia entrance by 18:45 at the latest (that's when the desk closes). There are stairs inside up to the first terrace, then the lifts do the rest. The ticket also covers the museums inside, for a week.

swaps.title: Cheaper, with a drink
swaps.body: The Capitoline museums' café terrace, a few minutes away, looks west over the domes, and part of it has a roof. No ticket needed: go in from Piazzale Caffarelli. Drinks at the counter are cheaper than at the tables.

rain.title: Kandinsky, open late
rain.body: A big Kandinsky show right on Piazza Venezia, mostly lent by the Centre Pompidou, open until 21:00 on Fridays. All colour and shapes, no art degree needed. Or sit out the rain under Terrazza Caffarelli's roof, which needs no ticket.
rain.move: Timed entry: book online. Last tickets 20:00.

stops.title: Pit stop
stops.body: Back to base. Showers, feet up, phones on charge. The other two land around now.

stops.title: Table for four
stops.body: Proper Roman pizza and the Roman pastas at the same table, so nobody has to choose. Start with supplì: pull one apart and the mozzarella stretches like an old phone cord, which is why they're called 'al telefono'. Then carbonara and a margherita. Sunday will thank us.
stops.move: Tables for four were still free on 8 October, but it fills up. I'll book for about 21:00 and move it once we know when they land. The carbonara is cooked to order and takes a while, so order it first.

swaps.title: If their flight is late
swaps.body: Loud, cheap, marble tables, open until around 2. No bookings; the queue thins out after 22:00. Worth a call first: +39 06 580 0919.

swaps.title: If they're stuck at Termini
swaps.body: A food hall inside the station. Everyone picks their own stall, and nobody needs a booking.

stops.title: One coin, then bed
stops.body: With all four of us: the Pantheon lit up, Sant'Ignazio's fake dome once more (open until 23:30 and empty by now), then Trevi. The ticket gates around the water close at 22:00, so after that it's free and much quieter. Gelato at Giolitti on the way home, open until midnight.
stops.move: Coin in your right hand, throw it over your left shoulder. Tradition says you'll come back to Rome. No sitting on the rim and no touching the water: the fines are real.

book.label: Pantheon tickets
book.detail: Both of us, named, 11:00–12:00 slot. €7, or €2 if EU and 18–25. I need your full name as it is on your ID.

book.label: Vittoriano rooftop
book.detail: Dated ticket, no time slot, good for 7 days. €18, or €5 if EU and 18–24.

book.label: Emma, table for four
book.detail: About 21:00, moved once the others have flight times. No prepayment; they hold the table 20 minutes.

book.label: Race confirmation letters
book.detail: Download, print, check for two green OKs and the wave time. Plus photo ID.

book.label: Thursday night checks
book.detail: Strikes (none listed for Rome transport as of 8 Oct) and Vittoriano closure notices.

practical.title: Tap to ride
practical.body: Buses, trams and metro take a contactless card or phone at the reader. €1.50 a ride, valid 100 minutes, capped at €8.50 a day. One card per person, and tap again on every bus.

practical.title: Free water everywhere
practical.body: The little iron fountains (nasoni) run drinking water. Block the spout with a finger and it shoots up out of a hole on top. Bring a bottle.

practical.title: Shoulders and knees
practical.body: Churches want them covered. A light scarf in the bag solves it.

practical.title: Trevi costs €2 now
practical.body: During the day, for the area right by the water. On Fridays it opens at 11:30; last entry 21:00, gates close at 22:00. Sitting on the rim costs €40–240.

practical.title: Don't sit on the Spanish Steps
practical.body: It's banned, with fines of up to €400.

practical.title: Pickpockets
practical.body: Termini, bus 64 and the Trevi crowd. Phone in the front pocket, bag zipped.

alsoOn.title: Rome Film Fest, day four
alsoOn.body: Red carpets at the Auditorium are free to watch from the steps, first come first served. There's a free shuttle from Termini.

alsoOn.title: Ara Pacis light show
alsoOn.body: Projections paint an Augustan altar back into its original colours. Fridays to Sundays only, at 20:00, 21:00 and 22:00, 40 people a show. €15 (€13 if EU and 25 or under).

alsoOn.title: Kandinsky until 21:00
alsoOn.body: Palazzo Bonaparte stays open until 21:00 on Fridays (last tickets 20:00). €18 + €1.50 online. Our rain plan for the evening.

budgetNote: EU and 18–24? The Pantheon drops to €2 and the Vittoriano to €5.

footer.line: Made for one Friday in Rome. Hours and prices checked on 8 October 2026; check again on Thursday.
